title: Sleeping in the Shade
bodyHtml:
The data in this problem are drawn from Ik, the native language of the Ik people who live on a narrow swath of land in the northeastern corner of Uganda, East Africa. (A map is provided below.) The people call their language Icétôd, which means ‘Ik-speech’ or ‘Ik-talk’ and is pronounced ee-CHAY-TOad or [ītʃétôd] in phonetic symbols. Approximately 7,500 people are native speakers of Ik.

The Ik phrases and sentences in this problem are written in the commonly used orthography. Keep in mind the following as you examine the data:

  • The digraph ts and the trigraph ts’ are used to represent two different consonant sounds in Ik.
  • A diacritic borrowed from the International Phonetic Alphabet has been added to the data to reflect a pronunciation feature relevant to the problem. The symbol is a small ring that appears below a letter. This diacritic reflects that the sound represented orthographically is pronounced without the vocal folds vibrating or, in less technical terms, is whispered by the native speakers of the language. Something similar happens in English when native speakers pronounce words like potato [pʰə̥ˈtʰeɪ̯ɾoʊ̯] and peculiar [pʰə̥ˈkʲuːliɚ] where the vowel in the first syllable becomes voiceless. To appreciate how this phonetic process works, try saying the word peculiar or potato with a pause between the first and second syllable of the word, and notice that your vocal folds do not begin vibrating until you pronounce the second syllable of the word. In the case of English, the vowel in the first syllable of words with this phonological structure is devoiced, which means it is pronounced without vocal fold vibration.

questions.partPrompt: Some argue that Ik does not have adjectives as a grammatical category of words in the same way that English does. Give the numbers (1-19) of two sentences or phrases that would make people think this.

hints.text: Ik does not put the subject first the way English does - look at which position in the Ik string the action word occupies. Then hunt for short repeated words (bee, na, ni, dii, ɲcie, ntsie) and for the endings on the longer words, especially the final vowel -a versus -o.

Three separate systems are at work. (1) Little words like na and ni link a noun to a word that describes it, and the choice between the two depends on whether the noun is one thing or several. (2) One short word always stands immediately after the action word and tells you about time. (3) The ring diacritic is not part of any word's spelling: compare where in an utterance it does and does not appear, and which vowel letters it never sits under.

Here is one safe counting step to get you started on the matching. Five Ik items begin with the same first word, Epa, and exactly five English translations mention sleeping - so the first word of an Ik sentence is the verb, and the subject comes after it. Sort both columns into groups by verb (sleep, come, go, love, chew) before you try to pair anything up; then inside each group use the extra words (length, the little word bee, possessives) to tell the members apart.

explanationHtml:
Step 1: Find the verb - it comes first

Count first words. Epa starts five Ik items (3, 8, 13, 15, 17), and exactly five English translations talk about sleeping (A, D, E, J, M). Mina/Minia starts three items, and three English sentences talk about loving. So an Ik clause begins with its verb, and the subject follows it: Ik order is roughly Verb - Subject - other stuff. That is why the word-for-word gloss of S1 in E2 starts with Sleeps.

Step 2: The little word bee marks the past

Three items contain bee right after the verb: 1, 9, 15. The three English translations with a past-tense verb are Father went, We came from Ethiopia and The dog slept in the hut. Compare the pair Atsa abaŋa Isopiao̥ ‘Father is coming from Ethiopia’ with Atsima bee Isopiao̥ ‘We came from Ethiopia’: same verb root Ats- ‘come’, and bee is what adds the pastness.

Step 3: Endings on the verb show who does it

The verb root Ats- ‘come’ shows up as Atsa (he/she/it), Atsia (I), Atsima (we), Atse̥ (command: Come!). The same endings appear on Min- ‘love’: Mina ‘he loves’, Minia ‘I love’, Minima ‘we love’. There is also a plural-subject ending -ta, which is why Zeƙwata in E4a goes with a plural subject.

Step 4: Nouns and their endings

-ika makes a noun plural: hoo/hoika ‘hut/huts’, oŋor-/oŋorika ‘elephant/elephants’. The final vowel also tells you the noun's job: a subject-like form ends in -a (oŋorḁ ‘the elephant’ as subject), while a form used for a place or accompaniment ends in -o (hoo̥ ‘in/from the hut’, kuruo̥ ‘in the shade’, oŋoro̥ ‘with the elephant’, Isopiao̥ ‘from Ethiopia’).

Step 5: na, ni, and possessives

ɲcie means ‘my’ and ntsie means ‘his/her’; they follow the noun, either bare or introduced by na. na and ni are relative words, roughly ‘which, that’: na after a singular noun, ni after a plural one (see item 11, which has plural hoika and ni). dii is ‘these’, leɓetse is ‘two’, gaana is ‘bad’, daa is ‘nice’, ɓets’a is ‘white’. Item 11 lines up piece by piece: huts - these - my - two - which - bad.

Step 6: Building the E3 and E4 answers

For ‘my huts’ you can either place the possessive straight after the noun or link it with the relative word, which is why E3b and E3c each have two correct forms. For ‘Father is coming from the nice hut’, start with the verb (‘he comes’), then the subject ‘father’, then the hut in its -o place form, then the describing word introduced by the singular relative word. In E4c the string is ‘we-love elephants which sleep’, which English can render either as a relative clause (elephants who sleep) or as a participle (sleeping elephants) - two structurally different translations of one Ik sentence.

Step 7: E5 - is ni optional before a numeral?

Item 11 shows the full string with ni before the last describing word, and the data also show describing words attached with no relative word at all. Both patterns are attested, so both P1 and P2 are fine: the answer is (c).

Step 8: E6 - where the ring appears

List every place the ring occurs and every place it does not. It never appears in the middle of an utterance - ŋoka, abaŋa, hoika and the rest are plain when other words follow them - and it appears on the very last vowel of an utterance instead. The one exception is item 19, which ends in i and carries no ring. Hence the official rule: Ik speakers devoice all vowels except for [i] in utterance-final position. Devoicing here is the same whispered effect described for English potato.

Step 9: E7 - where are the adjectives?

In Ik, words meaning ‘white’, ‘nice’ and ‘bad’ do not sit next to the noun the way English adjectives do; they are attached with the relative word na/ni, exactly the way a whole clause like ‘which sleeps’ is attached. That is, they behave like little verbs (‘which is-white’), which is the reason linguists argue Ik has no separate adjective class. The items that show this most clearly are 3, 11 and 13, and any two of those three count.
